newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China bonds steady in Asia, outlook still positive.
newsitem.headline: China bonds steady in Asia, outlook still positive.

text.p: Bonds issued by China overseas showed little reaction in Asian markets on Thursday to news of Deng Xiaoping's death, and analysts said the the outlook for Chinese credits remains positive.
"There really isn't any impact at all. If anything, the bonds are better bid because the uncertainty is out of the market," said a secondary market trader at a European bank in Singapore.
China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping died late on Wednesday.
China's global bond due 2006 was bid at 74 basis point over comparable U.S. Treasury bonds and offered at 71 basis points in Asia, unchanged from its level in New York overnight.
The China global bond due 2006 has been trading in the 70-75 basis point range for many weeks.
Bankers said China credits traded in the international market had not been seriously affected by reports over the last several days that Deng was gravely ill.
The story has been the same for issues that trade more locally, traders said.

Syndicate managers said Bank of China's high-profile HK$4 billion floating rate certificate of deposit issue due 2001 was trading at 40 basis points over the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate, unmoved from recent weeks.
"There's no selling pressure. The news (on Deng) has been pretty much absorbed," said a trader in Hong Kong.
While most Asian bonds have had a stellar year, China bonds have performed particularly well due to improved sentiment toward China in the international investment community.

For example, the China bond due 2006 was launched last July to yield 110 basis points over Treasuries. China's century bond, which was launched at 299 basis points over the benchmark a year ago is trading around 135 basis points over Treasuries now.
Deng's death does not change the positive outlook for China credits, analysts said.

"China's economy right now is very strong," said Donald Hanna, executive director, Asian Investment Research, at Goldman Sachs. The country is running a trade surplus, its foreign exchange reserves are very high, inflation is relatively low and growth is robust, Hanna said.

"The issues that are brought up by Deng's death are not so much to do with the strength of the economy but with the pace and manner in which reforms affecting economic growth continue going forward and the influence political reforms might have on that process," he said.
Any decline in China bond prices "would be a buying opportunity," a trader at a U.S. bank in Hong Kong said.
Traders said they would keep an eye on political developments in China in the wake of Deng's passing, but most said they did not anticipate a power struggle.

Rating agency Standard and Poor's Corp said its does not believe the transfer of power will lead to a major disruption in Chinese politics or a disruption in the continued development of the Chinese economy.
Speaking from New York, S&P China analyst Guido Cipriani said "The death of Deng will complete the de facto transfer of power to Communist Party leader Jiang Zemin."
He said the entrenched position of the leadership group should ensure overall policy stability during the transition.
S&P said it would not reassess China's BBB sovereign rating following Deng's death and that its outlook for the country's credit rating remains positive.
Moody's Investors Service also said that Deng's death should not affect the direction of China's economic policy and will have no impact on the country's A3 sovereign rating.
